s.text: About this app

FactSheet is a free guide to HIV, reproductive health and youth wellbeing. It has been rebuilt as a fast, offline-first native app and its health information is updated to reflect current global guidance (WHO, CDC, UNAIDS).
The information is for education and does not replace advice from a qualified health worker.
BE FACTUAL, BE INFORMED
HIVFactSheet App
is unique in the sense that it empowers the user with comprehensive HIV and Reproductive Health knowledge and information.
The app also connects the users with an online counselor who responds to their questions while referring them to health facilities whenever needed.
Lastly the app can be used as a reminder to the clinic appointments when a user sets.

What is ABORTION?
Is the termination of a pregnancy
Types of abortion
Spontaneous abortion
- usually termed as miscarriage
Induced abortion
– It is either safe or unsafe
An abortion can occur spontaneously due to complications during pregnancy or can be induced.
Importance of abortion counseling
When a woman is faced with an unintended pregnancy she needs a professional counseling to enable her decide whether to:-
Keep the pregnancy
Give birth safely then either keep the child or give the child to adoption
Choose to have a safe termination
LAWS ON ABORTION
Article 26 (4) :
Abortion is not permitted unless in the opinion of a health professional
Only if -
A need arises for emergency treatment or
When the life of the mother is in danger or
If its permitted by any other written law
Article 43 (1a) :
Every person has a right to the highest attainable standard of health, which includes the right to health care services including reproductive health (
post abortion care
) Sexual Offences management act provides for an option for a safe termination if a woman has gotten pregnant as a result of sexual offence (
rape, defilement or incest
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT ABORTION
What is a safe abortion?
Safe abortion is termination of a pregnancy by a health care provider qualified in providing the services while observing proper health standards.
What is an unsafe abortion?

The World Health Organization defines unsafe abortion as a procedure for terminating an unintended pregnancy carried out either by persons lacking the necessary skills or in an environment that does not conform to minimal medical standards, or both. Unsafe abortions may lead to complications such as perforations of the uterus, retained placentas, severe bleeding, cervical wounds, rampant infections, poisoning, shock and gangrene.
What is post-abortion care?

In settings where abortion is legally restricted or access to services is limited, women with unwanted pregnancies often resort to unsafe abortions and subsequently require urgent medical attention to treat complications. Women may also suffer incomplete spontaneous abortions (miscarriages) or complications from a safe abortion that require medical attention.
Post abortion care,

a term originated by Ipas in the early 1990s, is an approach for reducing deaths and injuries from incomplete and unsafe abortions and their related complications. Post abortion care is an integral component of comprehensive abortion care and includes five essential elements:
Treatment of incomplete and unsafe abortion and complications
Counselling to identify and respond to women’s emotional and physical health needs
Contraceptive and family-planning services to help women prevent future unwanted pregnancies and abortions
Reproductive and other health services that are preferably provided on-site or via referrals to other accessible facilities

Community and service-provider partnerships to prevent unwanted pregnancies and unsafe abortions, to mobilize resources to ensure timely care for abortion complications, and to make sure health services meet community expectations and needs.
What is the difference between a spontaneous and induced abortion?
Spontaneous abortion

is the loss of pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation without outside intervention. Induced abortion, or abortion by choice, is a procedure that is done to end a pregnancy. Most induced abortions are done in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Who may provide safe abortions?
According to Kenyan law, safe abortions may be provided by qualified health care providers while adhering to required medical standards. Kenyan Law and Abortion According to Kenya law,

an induced abortion may be performed on recommendation of a qualified health service provider. According to article 26 (4) of the Constitution of Kenya “abortion is not permitted unless, in the opinion of a trained health professional, there is need for emergency treatment, or the life or the health of the mother is in danger, or if permitted by any other written law.”
Can a woman get pregnant after having a safe abortion?
Yes, it is possible if they have sexual intercourse without using any contraceptive method.
How long will a woman feel pain after having a safe abortion?

Women experience very little pain when abortion is done in a safe way by a qualified health care provider at a health facility. Minimal discomfort, however, may last for about three days. How soon can a woman start having sex after having an abortion? As soon as she feels comfortable having sex, but it is recommended that she doesn’t have sex for one week and avoid putting anything like tampons in the vagina to reduce chances of getting infections.
What are the chances that a woman could die if she has safe abortion?

Chances of a woman dying from safe abortion are almost nil if done by a trained health care provider. However complications may arise as a result of other previous medical issues a client may have had but not from the abortion itself.
Can there be complications after having a safe abortion?
Chances of complications are very low after having a safe abortion. In case of any complications like severe bleeding, one is advised to seek medical attention.
Can safe abortion procedure interfere with a woman’s walking style?
No, it does not. But rarely, the discomfort from the procedure may temporarily make normal walking a challenge.
Can safe abortion lead to a woman having subsequent pregnancy growing out of the uterus and suffering miscarriage?

No, safe abortion does not harm a woman in any way neither does it cause ectopic pregnancies. After having safe abortion, a woman is able to conceive any other time she chooses to, carry the pregnancy in a normal way to term and deliver a healthy child if there is no other medical condition that affects future fertility .
Does abortion mean removal of the uterus?
No, safe abortion is not the removal of the uterus. Safe abortion is the removal of the products of a pregnancy from the uterus and not the removal of the uterus.
Can a health care provider be arrested for performing an abortion?

One cannot be arrested for performing safe abortion if the person is a trained health care provider working within a health facility that meets the set standards of health. According to the Kenya constitution, safe abortion can be performed by a health care provider if the mental, social and physical health of a woman is in danger. A health care provider is a trained doctor, clinical officer, nurse or a midwife.
Can one be arrested for seeking a safe abortion?

According to the Kenya constitution abortion is not permitted on demand however safe abortion can be performed by a health care provider if the mental, social and physical health of a woman is in danger. Women seeking abortions should consult a trained health care provider to determine if induced abortion is an option for her. Seeking abortion outside of the formal health care system can put women at risk of arrest.

Latest guidance
You can now test at home with an
HIV self-test kit
, as well as at clinics, pharmacies and through community outreach. A reactive self-test is always confirmed at a health facility.
A WORD ON TESTING
HIV testing – widely available
Testing should always be preceded by pre-test counseling and followed by posttest counseling
Life changing effects:
Medical
Psychological stress
Social-discrimination, loss of a job or family
Available Test
- Antibody tests
Rapid tests
Noninvasive Rapid tests
Elisa
- Tests that detect the viral elements
Western blot
P24 antigen
PCR
Latest guidance
Testing is recommended for anyone who wants to know their status, and especially people with a new or multiple partners, another STI, TB, or who could benefit from PrEP.
HIV self-test kits
make testing easy and private.
WHO SHOULD GO FOR HIV TESTING
Anyone who is sexuality active and:  Had sex with a person whose HIV status doesn’t know.  Had sex with someone who is HIV positive
Anyone who share used needles and syringes.
Couple who want to start a having sex.
Pregnant mothers and their partners, to protect their baby from HIV infection.
Why test

Testing is the gateway to same-day treatment if positive (reaching an undetectable, untransmittable viral load, U=U) or to prevention such as PrEP if negative. Free HIV self-test kits are widely available.
WHY GO FOR A HIV TEST
HIV Testing is an entry point for Risk reduction
Testing positive allows you seek care and treatment services.
Counselling can help you accept your status
Latest guidance

If one partner is HIV-positive, they can take ART to reach an undetectable viral load so HIV is not passed on (U=U), while the HIV-negative partner can use PrEP. With ART in pregnancy, nearly all babies are born HIV-free.
WHY GET TESTED AS A COUPLE
If you both test negative, It will motivate you to remain faithful to each other or use a condom correctly when having sex.
You and your partner can discuss concerns about your sex life, and how to avoid getting infected
If one of you test positive, you will be advised on how to continue a normal life without the other getting infected. You will also be advised on how to get negative children
IF TESTED POSITIVE, HOW CAN I LIVE A NORMAL LIFE?
Continue going for counselling
Seek treatment for infections as soon as possible
Take ART and eat well
Go for PMTCT if you are pregnant to ensure your baby is safe.
Allow your family to care for you or help
Join a support group with other people like you and be encouraged.
Protect yourself from getting reinfections.
Seek community service.
Latest guidance

The window period is now shorter: 4th-generation tests detect most infections within 2-6 weeks. A negative result after a possible exposure should still be confirmed once the window has passed (about 3 months for antibody-only rapid tests).
WINDOW PERIOD
After HIV infection there is a delay before HIV antibodies become detectable in the blood ( 1-3) weeks)
Rapid or Elisa tests will be negative
Latest Elisa tests can detect infection at 2 weeks
PCR can detect infection at approximately two weeks after infection
This is an important point to remember when dealing with a negative test- window period must be excluded before confirming the result as negative
After you start an HIV regimen, use a variety of strategies to maintain adherence.
To maintain adherence over the long term, try some of the following strategies:
Use a 7-day pill box. Once a week, fill the pill box with your HIV medicines for the entire week.
Take your HIV medicines at the same time every day.
Set the alarm on your cell phone to remind you to take your medicines. (An alarm clock or timer works too.)to bookmark your HIV medicines, make notes, and set daily pill reminders.
Ask your family members, friends, or coworkers to remind you to take your medicines.
Keep your medicines nearby. Keep a back-up supply of medicines at work or in your purse or briefcase.
Plan ahead for changes in your daily routine, including weekends and holidays. If you’re going away, pack enough medicine to last the entire trip.

Use an app or an online or paper medicine diary to stay on track. Enter the name of each medicine; include the dose, number of pills to take, and when to take them. Record each medicine as you take it. Reviewing your diary will help you identify the times that you’re most likely to forget to take your medicines.

Keep all of your medical appointments. Use a calendar to keep track of your appointments. If you run low on medicines before your next appointment, call your health care provider to renew your prescriptions.
Get additional tips on adherence by joining a support group for people living with HIV.
What should I do if I forget to take my HIV medicines?

Unless your health care provider tells you otherwise, take the medicine you missed as soon as you realize you skipped it. But if it’s almost time for the next dose of the medicine, don’t take the missed dose and instead just continue on your regular medication schedule. Don’t take a double dose of a medicine to make up for a missed dose.
Discuss medication adherence at each appointment with your health care provider.
Tell your health care provider if you’re having difficulty following your regimen.
Don’t forget to mention any side effects you’re having.
Side effects from HIV medicines are a major reason why medication adherence can be difficult.
Let your health care provider know if your regimen is too complicated to follow.
Your health care provider may simplify your regimen by including fewer HIV medicines or by reducing the number of times a day you need to take your HIV medicines.
Discuss any issues that are causing you to skip medicines.
Your health care provider can recommend resources to help you deal with the issues.
Current treatment
Alongside NRTIs, NNRTIs and protease inhibitors,
integrase inhibitors (INSTIs) such as dolutegravir
are now a core class. The global first-line regimen is TLD (TDF + 3TC + DTG).
ART is started for everyone at diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count or symptoms.
Three main groups of antiretroviral
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors 158 (
NRTIs
Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (
NNRTIs
) and
Protease inhibitors (
PIs
Each group of drugs works at a different point in the life cycle of the virus within the cell.
The decision to begin antiretroviral therapy in an HIV-infected person is determined by that person’s
clinical, virologic, and immunologic condition.
Antiretroviral therapy often is changed when an HIV-infected child or adult experiences clinical, virologic, or immunologic failure. Among the numerous barriers to treatment are
cost, time commitment, compliance, and home environment.
Therapeutic Goals
The primary goal of antiretroviral therapy
is to improve the health and prolong the life of the HIV- infected child or adult. This is achieved by interfering with the ability of the virus to replicate or reproduce inside the body.
When the virus is unable to replicate, damage to the immune system is minimized. Because the immune system is functioning more normally, the treated individual is less susceptible to
opportunistic infections, malignancies, and other illnesses.
HIV-infected patients receiving
antiretroviral therapy
also are less likely to develop other complications associated with HIV/AIDS,
such as wasting syndrome and encephalopathy (a disorder of the brain).
Most patients taking effective antiretroviral therapy will live longer than they would without medications.
The CD4+ cell
The CD4+ cell count
measures the concentration
of a particular type of lymphocyte, the T-helper cell, in a specified amount of the patient’s blood.
The CD4+ cell is severely affected by HIV infection.

In the body, HIV attaches to and enters CD4+ cells. Once inside, the virus subverts the CD4+ cell’s replication machinery, turning it into a virus factory. In the process of copying itself, the virus destroys the CD4+ cell. Often when a patient begins antiretroviral therapy, the CD4+
count will increase a reflection of the immune system’s improved ability to fight infection.
Determining a patient’s CD4+ cell count at regular intervals allows the health professional to monitor
the strength of the patient’s immune system.

Successful antiretroviral therapy will cause the CD4+ cell count to rise and then remain elevated during therapy. A decrease in the concentration of CD4+ cells may represent failure of antiretroviral therapy.
Latest guidance
For people on effective treatment with a sustained undetectable viral load, HIV cannot be passed to sexual partners (U=U). Condoms still protect against other STIs and pregnancy.
How did I get the HIV virus?

There are many ways a person can contract the HIV virus. Sometimes, children can contract the HIV virus from their mother during child birth. Other times, children can receive blood transfusions with the virus in the extra blood. HIV can also be transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse. In the past, we did not have drugs to prevent the passing of the virus from mother to child and didn’t have appropriate tools to test blood before transfusions. You cannot change that you were infected with the HIV virus, but it is important to recognize how you can manage the HIV in your system. You can best manage the HIV virus by taking your medicines daily. You can prevent passing the virus to anyone else by taking your medicines, not engaging in unprotected sex, and taking care of any open wounds you may have.
How long do I need to take the medicines?

Sometimes, you may feel like taking medicines is cumbersome and difficult to swallow. You should continue to take your medicines daily as the doctor or clinical officer has prescribed to you. If you stop taking your medicines, your soldier cells may become weak and the virus can take over your body and make you very sick. By taking your medicines, your soldier cells stay strong and you won’t get sick!
What Does CD4 count mean?
The CD4 count is the number of healthy soldier cells you have in your blood. The more healthy soldier cells you have in your blood, the better you will feel!
Can this disease be cured?

Right now we do not have a way to cure this disease. We cannot kill it and remove it from the body. But the good news is that your medicines can control the virus, so the virus will not harm you. The medicines can keep the virus sleeping. HIV can be controlled by strictly taking medications and following doctor’s instructions. Researchers and doctors are working to find a cure for this disease, but right now there is no cure, anywhere in the world. When you hear that there is a cure, this is false information.
How long will I live?

If you take your meds regularly, follow doctors’ instructions well and take good care of yourself —like eating good foods, getting good sleep, making healthy decisions and staying away from risky behaviors such as drug and alcohol use and unprotected sexual intercourse—you can grow up to be an adult, have a family, be healthy and achieve your dreams in life.
Am I dying?

People who have HIV will not die very soon if they take good care of themselves and take their medications regularly. They can still live normally and choose their own way to live. Many children who started taking ARV drugs in their childhood have lived positive lives and have attended schools, become doctors and nurses, have families, and accomplish many things in their adult lives.
Can I have a boyfriend/ girlfriend or get married one day?

Yes, you can have a boyfriend/girlfriend or get married when you are an adult and ready. The foundation of a couple’s life together is built on understanding and trusting each other. Both your health and your partner’s health should be discussed in a trusting and honest way. Your counselor can help you to prepare for talking about this with the person you choose
Should I tell a boyfriend/girlfriend that I have HIV? If so, when?

If you have a boyfriend or girlfriend, you should disclose your status when you feel you truly trust that person. This is a very careful decision and you should take your time. Refrain from engaging in any unprotected sexual behaviors until you have told the person. Remember, if you care about this person, you should help protect him or her and not transmit the virus. Focus on strengthening your relationship with trust and caring before you disclose your status or engage in adult behaviors.
Is it necessary that I should be boyfriend/girlfriend, or married, only with a HIV positive person?

If you have HIV and your partner does not, that is okay! But you need to use appropriate protection, so you do not transmit the virus to your partner. Please consider talking to a counselor or a doctor for appropriate advice in how to manage HIV and not transmit it to your partner. Your life as a couple will require understanding and safe practices; the doctor will give you good directions.
It’s okay to have Questions!

Being diagnosed with HIV can be a scary experience, and you may find yourself asking many questions. It is important to know that you are not alone and there are many people including your doctors and counselors to help you with your challenges. In this pamphlet are some of the most frequent questions asked by adolescents who have recently learned they are HIV positive.

Young people on effective treatment who stay undetectable cannot pass HIV to sexual partners (U=U). Condoms still protect against other STIs and pregnancy.
How can you tell if someone is sick?

Sometimes, people can show signs of being sick through physical symptoms, like losing weight and becoming thin, rashes, or coughing. However, many times people may have an illness, but manage the illness with taking medications. With proper management of the illness, you may not be able to tell if a person is sick.
Why am I taking medicines if I am not physically sick?

Sometimes, we need to take medicines to keep our bodies healthy. You are prescribed pills even though you are not showing physical signs of sickness because there is still an illness or sickness in your body that could cause problems if you are not taking the medicines. Your body has soldier cells to help fight illnesses and keep your body healthy and strong. The pills prescribed to you help make your soldier cells strong.
Why am I taking medicines and my siblings are not taking medicines?

Each person’s body can react differently to illnesses. For instance, one of your siblings may develop a cough during the rainy season, but you don’t! Your siblings may not have to take pills every day because their soldier cells that fight off illness are already strong. You need to do what is right for your body alone. Since your body needs to have strong soldier cells, remember to take the pills to strengthen your soldier cells!

Other times, children can receive blood transfusions with the virus in the extra blood. HIV can also be transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse. You will not transmit the virus to anyone else if you do not engage in unprotected sex, you take your medicines daily, and you take care of any open wounds you may have.

Sometimes, you may feel like taking medicines is cumbersome and difficult to swallow. You should continue to take your medicines, daily, as the doctor or clinical officer has prescribed to you. If you stop taking your medicines, your soldier cells may become weak and the virus can take over your body and make you very sick. By taking your medicines, your soldier cells stay strong and you won’t get sick!
What Does CD4 count mean?
The CD4 count is the number of healthy soldier cells you have in your blood. The more healthy soldier cells you have in your blood, the better you will feel!

Right now we do not have way to cure this disease. We cannot kill it and remove it from the body. But the good news is that your medicines can control the virus, so the virus will not harm you. The medicines can keep the virus sleeping. HIV can be controlled by strictly taking medications and following doctor’s instructions. Researchers and doctors are working to find a cure for this disease, but right now there is no cure, anywhere in the world. When you hear that there is a cure, this is false information.
How long will I live?

If you take your medicines regularly, follow doctors’ instructions well, and take good care of yourself (by eating good foods, getting good sleep, making healthy decisions and staying away from risky behaviors such as drugs, alcohol, and unprotected sexual intercourse), you can grow up to be an adult, be healthy, and achieve your dreams in life.
Am I dying?

People who have HIV will not die very soon if they take good care of themselves and take their medications regularly. They can still live normally and choose their own way to live. Many children who started taking ARV drugs in their childhood have lived positive lives and have attended schools, become doctors and nurses, have families, and accomplish many things in their adult lives.

Here are some general disclosure tips:
Be selective.
Choosing whom to tell or not tell is your personal decision. It's your choice and your right.
Consider
the five "W's"
when thinking about disclosure:
who, what, when, where and why.

Who do you need to tell? What do you want to tell them about your HIV infection, and what are you expecting from the person you are disclosing your HIV status to? When should you tell them? Where is the best place to have this conversation? Why are you telling them?
Easy does it.
In most situations, you can take your time to consider who to tell and how to tell them.
Consider whether there is a real purpose for you to tell this person or if you are simply feeling anxious and want to "dump" your feelings.
Telling people indiscriminately may affect your life in ways you haven't considered.
Having feelings of uncertainty about disclosure is a very common reaction.
You have a virus.
You don't have anything to apologize for simply because you are HIV positive.
Keep it simple.
You don't have to tell the story of your life.
Avoid isolating yourself.

If you are unable to tell close friends, family members or other loved ones about your HIV status, allow yourself to draw upon the support and experience of others in the HIV community. Consider joining a support group or an online forum, such as the POZ Forums.
There's no perfect roadmap for how to disclose. Trust your instinct, not your fears.
Even if the response you receive in a specific situation, doesn't go the way you'd hoped, you're going to survive it and your life will go on.
Millions of others have dealt with this experience and have found their way through it. You will get through it too.
Latest guidance
HIV self-testing
lets you test privately at home; a reactive result is confirmed at a clinic. If positive, ART starts the same day and leads to an undetectable, untransmittable viral load (U=U).
Partners & Spouses
The issue of disclosing your status to your partner or significant other can be complex.
If you've had unprotected sex with your partner, it's important to alert him or her to the fact that he or she may be at risk and should get tested.
Regardless of your partner's decision to test and his or her results, by disclosing, you're making him or her aware of the need to practice safer sex together in the future.
You might also want to tell your partner in an effort to get the emotional support you need.
It's important to have someone to listen to your concerns, to offer suggestions, and to just simply be there.
While some people fear becoming a burden when they have health problems, sharing your experiences can often be an opportunity for building a deeper intimacy and a stronger partnership.
It's perfectly normal to experience anxiety about telling a partner.

Before he or she can respond to your needs, your partner may first feel anxiety about his or her own HIV status (which can only be addressed through HIV testing) and may also feel angry and upset if the HIV infection occurred sexually, outside of the relationship.
Disclosing your HIV status can add strain on the relationship so it’s important for you to give some thought as to when and how to disclose.
Depending on the nature of your relationship, you might want to consider some professional couples counseling.
It's important for you to be aware of what the laws are in your state with regard to contact tracing and partner notification.
Contact tracing refers to the efforts of government agencies to identify any and all persons who might be at risk of contracting HIV from an infected person.
Partner notification refers to information conveyed to spouses, sexual partners, needle sharers and others who might be at risk for HIV infection.
The laws regarding this vary from state to state. In many states, partner notification can be done anonymously through the state's Department of Health.
The Department of Health in your state is a good source of information about what the legal procedure is in your state and how it might apply to you.
General contact tracing and partner notification issues to consider:

In general, physicians may breach patient confidentiality in this situation and notify a sexual or needle-sharing partner of an individual's HIV infection who is at identifiable risk of infection, as long as they act in good faith and offer only the information necessary to help the notified person protect against future risk of infection or seek medical treatment.
These guidelines do not require that a physician disclose the name of the person who might be putting an individual at risk, although in some instances that identity will be obvious.
These guidelines do not justify disclosures about HIV information to insurers, employers, schools or other institutions.
Efforts at contact tracing need not breach medical confidentiality with regard to the HIV-positive person. They need only advise people that they may have been exposed to HIV.
Latest guidance
U = U — Undetectable = Untransmittable.
Someone on HIV treatment with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV to sexual partners. This is backed by global scientific consensus (WHO, CDC, UNAIDS).
You can date and have a full sex life. On effective treatment you are undetectable and cannot pass HIV on; a partner can also use PrEP.
The real benefit of disclosing to a date or to a casual or anonymous sex partner may be a personal one.

It takes strength of character to be honest in such a circumstance. At the same time, telling someone you are HIV positive at the beginning of a possible relationship or before having sex puts you in a vulnerable position.
It's never easy to predict if you'll receive a positive or negative response.
Despite the fact that most people know about safe sex and how the virus is transmitted, fear and stigma are still a reality in relation to HIV, and disclosure can stir up very strong emotions.
Your status may deter some people from proceeding further in a relationship with you.
General dating and sexual partner disclosure issues to consider:
Keep what you say as simple and as direct as possible.
Give yourself credit if you have been practicing safer sex with the sexual partner you're disclosing your status to. You are already behaving responsibly with that person.
If the person you're disclosing to reacts negatively, remember that's only one person. Not everyone is going to react the same way.
Remember

that you should give the person you're disclosing your status to some time to process the information. Whatever their reaction may be at first, whether negative or positive, be aware that reactions can change in time.
Family
If you have a good relationship with your family, disclosing to them may lead to an even stronger relationship.
Your family is likely to be concerned about your future. You may find yourself educating them about HIV, as well as giving them emotional support.
As they come to see that you're getting on with your life, and that your life is still good, their anxieties are likely to ease.
Your family can be a good source of support depending on the nature of your relationship with them.
Realistically, you also have to consider that if your relationship with your family has been less than ideal in the past, this news may further strain relations, at least for a while.
HIV-positive parents face different and difficult decisions concerning disclosure to their children.
These include important considerations of the prognosis of parental health and the matter of custody planning for underage children.
Understanding the implications of HIV/AIDS may be beyond younger children. Decisions must be made about what and when to disclose.
Friends
Studies show that most people disclose their HIV diagnosis to close friends within days of learning the news themselves.
Some people are more informed about HIV than others. A close friend may be able to offer new ways of thinking about your situation.
A friend's greatest contribution may be simply listening to you.

While most friends will respect that what you have revealed was told in confidence, you need to be aware that your HIV status may end up becoming the subject of gossip among your other friends and acquaintances.
In this situation, as in other difficult times in life, some friendships will endure and even deepen while others will fade away.
If you have a tight-knit family or social group, or you live in a small community or a rural area, confidentiality may be harder to maintain.
You might consider discussing with a counselor or some trusted person outside of your regular life about how to proceed.
General tips to consider when disclosing to family and friends:
Keep what you say as simple and as direct as possible.
Tell them you have something important to tell them.
Offer to answer any questions they may have.
Let them know they don't have to worry about your health.
If you have particular HIV-related issues or concerns that you're trying to sort out, let them know.
Request that what you're going to discuss be kept in confidence.
Ask them to be there for you.
Tell them how much they mean to you and how much you love them.
Don't be afraid to show your feelings and to express how important this issue is for you.
Disclosure in the Workplace
Co-Workers
Sometimes strong friendships develop with co-workers. In such situations, it's natural to want to tell a co-worker friend with whom you feel particularly close about your HIV status.
There may also be times when you're feeling particularly upset or stressed about something related to your status and have the impulse to disclose what's on your mind.
Even with a co-worker who's a good friend, give careful consideration to disclosing your positive status.
There's a balance to be maintained between the natural exchanges which occur in a friendship and protecting your need for privacy.
Be aware that even what you've said in confidence may still end up becoming the subject of gossip in the workplace.
When that happens, gossip can move up and down in the chain of command in the workplace, with unforeseen results that may have serious consequences.
Once you have disclosed your status, it's very hard—if not impossible—to take the information back.
Your co-worker friend may very well live up to your best expectations. But you have to be prepared to deal with potential disappointments as well.
General tips to consider with regard to the workplace:
Tell the person you have something important to tell them.
Stress that what you're going to discuss be kept in the strictest confidence.
Keep what you say as simple and as direct as possible.
Tell them why you want them to know.
Let them know you are sorting out issues related to your HIV status and their support is important to you.
Employers
If you're applying for a job, prospective employers do not have the right to make inquiries about your health or the existence of a disability prior to a conditional job offer.
However, they may legally inquire if you are aware of any physical limitation that would interfere with your ability to perform the essential functions of the job.

In a situation where an HIV-related illness is interfering with your work to the extent that it might place your employment in jeopardy, arranging to sit down privately with your boss and revealing your situation may be the way to go.
You might even consider bringing a letter from your doctor explaining the current state of your condition, and how it might affect your ability to perform your job.
General tips to consider with regard to employers:
Unless your HIV status affects your current ability to perform your job, you are under no legal obligation to disclose your status to your employer.
Consider very carefully what your purpose is for disclosing your status to your employer.
If you do disclose, tell the person you want to speak with that you have something important to discuss with them.
Stress that you're requesting that what you're going to discuss be kept in strict confidence.
Be mindful that a request for confidentially is not an absolute guarantee that it will be respected.
Some employers will rise to the occasion and be supportive. Others may be disappointing in their responses, and you will understandably feel hurt and angry.
Keep what you say as simple and as direct as possible.
Tell them you are receiving appropriate health care.
Mention if you may need a particular accommodation, such as occasional time off for a medical appointment.
Tell your boss that you will make every effort to insure that your work is properly covered and that you're committed to doing your job reliably and well.
Medical-related employer decisions about HIV (or any other disability) must be based on facts about you, not simply an employer's opinions about HIV.
Disclosure to Medical and Other Healthcare Providers

Your primary care physician needs to know about your HIV status. But in the course of your life, you will likely have occasions to visit different doctors and other health care professionals, sometimes for health matters that are not related to HIV. With other health care providers you have more of a choice whether or not to disclose.

For instance, there's no particular reason your podiatrist needs to know you are HIV positive. But in the case of your optometrist or your dentist, while you're not legally bound to disclose, by having that information he or she may be able to identify certain health problems.
All medical providers are supposed to be take "universal precautions," which means special procedures to protect themselves against any transmissible infection, not just HIV.

Health care providers cannot deny their services to someone simply because the person is HIV-positive. If a doctor or other health care provider is uncomfortable treating someone with HIV and makes that known in whatever way to you, be aware that you have legal recourse in such situations.
As far as disclosure of your HIV-related information is concerned, bear in mind that it's generally permitted only after you have signed an approved special HIV release form.
General tips to consider with regard to medical and health care providers:
All health care providers are bound by confidentiality laws.
By telling a doctor, a nurse or other health care providers, you do give up a degree of privacy, but that does not release them from adhering to laws regarding confidentiality.

Your status should be treated as privileged information. If, for instance, a doctor's employee discusses details with you that another patient might overhear, politely request that such conversations be discussed in private.
A hospital or other health care provider may share HIV information with a patient's insurance company if the information is necessary to pay for medical care.

If you're in doubt about whether you have to reveal your status for either medical or insurance purposes, or indeed legally for any other reason, call your local Department of Health or AIDS service organization. In some instances you may learn that it's necessary to disclose in order to have access to medical resources and services.
Latest guidance
Modern 4th-generation antigen/antibody tests detect most infections within about 2-6 weeks
— far sooner than older tests. Nucleic-acid (viral load) tests detect even earlier. HIV self-testing is also widely available.
HOW IS THE TEST USED?
The test is helpful in several areas:

For medical researchers, the test proved that HIV is never “latent” but is always multiplying. Many people with no symptoms of AIDS and high CD4 cell counts also had high viral loads. If the virus was latent, the test wouldn’t have found any HIV in the blood.

The test can be used for diagnosis , because it can detect a viral load a few days after HIV infection. This is better than the standard HIV (antibody) test, which can be “negative” for 2 to 6 months after HIV infection. ( Fact Sheet 102 has more information on HIV antibody testing. )
For prognosis , For prognosis, viral load can help predict how fast HIV disease progresses without treatment. The higher the viral load, the faster the disease progression.
For prevention, viral load predicts how easy it is to transmit HIV to someone else. The higher the viral load, the higher the risk of transmitting HIV.

For managing therapy , the test shows treatment is controlling the virus. Current guidelines ( Fact Sheet 404 ) suggest measuring baseline (pre-treatment) viral load. Treatment is “working” if it lowers viral load by at least 90% within 8 weeks. The viral load should continue to drop to less than 50 copies within 6 months. The viral load should be measured within 2 to 8 weeks after treatment is started or changed. It should be monitored every 6 months after that for patients with good adherence who have an undetectable viral load and have been clinically stable on their treatment for 2 or 3 years. According to the guidelines, treatment failure is indicated by a confirmed viral load above 200 copies while adherent to treatment.
HOW ARE CHANGES IN VIRAL LOAD MEASURED?

Repeated tests of the same blood sample can give results that vary by a factor of 3. This means that a meaningful change would be a drop to less than 1/3 or an increase to more than 3 times the previous test result. For example, a change from 200,000 to 600,000 is within the normal variability of the test. A drop from 50,000 to 10,000 would be significant. The most important change is to reach an undetectable viral load.

Viral load changes are often described as “log” changes. This refers to scientific notation, which uses powers of 10. For example, a 2-log drop is a drop of 102 or 100 times. A drop from 60,000 to 600 would be a 2-log drop.
"VIRAL LOAD “BLIPS”

Occasionally, patients sometimes went from undetectable to a low level (usually less than 500) and then returned to undetectable. These “blips” do not indicate virologic failure or that the virus is developing resistance.
Latest guidance
Everyone diagnosed starts ART immediately (treat-all).
U = U — Undetectable = Untransmittable.
Someone on HIV treatment with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV to sexual partners. This is backed by global scientific consensus (WHO, CDC, UNAIDS).
WHAT DO THE NUMBERS MEAN?

There are no “magic” numbers for viral loads. We don’t know how long you’ll stay healthy with any particular viral load. All we know so far is that lower is better and seems to mean a longer, healthier life. US and World Health Organization treatment guidelines strongly recommend that all HIV-positive people be offered treatment.
People on antiretroviral treatment with undetectable viral loads are extremely unlikely to pass the virus on to others.
ARE THERE LIMITATIONS WITH THE VIRAL LOAD TEST?

Only about 2% of the HIV in your body is in the blood. The viral load test does not measure how much HIV is in body tissues like the lymph nodes, spleen, or brain. HIV levels in lymph tissue and semen go down when blood levels go down, but not at the same time or the same rate.

The viral load test results can be thrown off if your body is fighting an infection, or if you have just received an immunization (like a flu shot). You should not have blood taken for a viral load test within four weeks of any infection or immunization.
Definitions
What is Adolescence?

Adolescence is the time between childhood and adulthood. It is the period during which a young person develops from a child into an adult. We usually consider adolescence between ages 10 to 19 years. This is a time that is marked by growth and change. Adolescents have changes in their bodies, in their thinking, and in their emotions.
What is Puberty?

The changes that occur in your body during adolescence are called puberty. Puberty means that your body is becoming a mature adult body. Having a mature adult body means that your body grows, your body begins to look like an adult body, and your body becomes capable of being pregnant or fathering a child.
How do I go through this stage successfully?
Accept the stage. Being an adolescent is a normal part of becoming an adult.
Accept your body’s changes. The changes in your body show that your body is healthy and strong.
Try to enjoy the journey of growing into an adult and having your opinions change Share any information, questions or disturbing issues with a trusted person
Be active and engage in healthy activities Seek and ask for advice from trusted sources such as a counselor, a parent, or a teacher
Being healthy means eating good foods, exercising your body, and taking medicines that your doctor has recommended for you.
Physical Changes

The changes in your body are caused by changes in the amounts of hormones that your body produces. This can make your body have increased odors, increased sweat, and other discharge. Girls also begin to have menstruation. For both girls and boys, it is especially important to maintain proper hygiene throughout puberty. Remember to wash your body daily
Social Changes
During adolescence, you may find that your relationships with your peers begin to change. You may
Start to become attracted to a friend of the opposite sex
Act shy towards this person or find it difficult to talk to them
Become interested in different hobbies or sports
Spend time with different groups of friends
Some of your friends or peers may start to change
What do I do if my friends are engaging in risky behaviors?

Sometimes, your friends may start to do things that may harm themselves or others. They might want to have sex without protection or drink alcohol. These friends may try to pressure you into doing the same risky behaviors. It is up to you to decide where your morals lie and how you will interact with these friends. You can ask yourself: Do these friends care about my future? Do these friends value the same morals that I value?
What do I do if I realize that my friends are talking about me?
You cannot control what people say or think about you. Remember that you are in control of your own emotional reactions and how you treat people.
During adolescence your relationships with your family may change.
As you get older, your parents may expect you to have more responsibilities.
You may desire more independence from your parents or guardians and your siblings.
You may not enjoy the games you used to love to play with your younger siblings.
You may not want to spend time with your family as you used to
Support Network

No matter what your situation is, it is good to have a social support system. Many people find that talking with certain people in their lives helps them to digest information or to handle stressful situations. The people in your life that you view as supportive and helpful are called your support system. It is helpful to identify some key people in your personal support system. During adolescence, your support system may change as your peers are also growing into new people. Even as you change and grow, you can find people you trust with information, ideas, and secrets. These people may be parents, caregivers, brother or sisters, close friends, grandparents or others who are close to you.

Having HIV does not STOP you from Living a Full and Health Life
With the right treatment and care, you can expect to live just as long as someone who doesn’t have HIV.
There’s a lot you can do to take care of yourself and feel fitter, healthier and happier.
If you have any questions, talk to your healthcare professional about nutrition, exercise, mental health or any of the other issues covered here.
Taking HIV treatment
Current treatment for HIV is not a cure for the virus, but it can keep HIV under control and this keeps your immune system strong.
In the past, older HIV drugs had serious side-effects, but treatment with modern HIV drugs is much better.
If a side-effect doesn’t go away and is affecting your quality of life, you should be able to change to a different drug .
Once you start HIV treatment , taking it every day is important to keep yourself well. Talk to your healthcare professional if you are having any problems taking treatment.
Overall approach
Your immune system can be strengthened by medical treatment, food, rest and exercise.
You can cope much better if you are happy and feel productive.
Emotional support and a positive attitude will help you to avoid depression.
A lot can also be done to avoid the devastating effects that illness and death have on families and children.
At the moment families and sometimes just individuals, cope with HIV and AIDS without much community support.
In most cases, very few people know that someone is HIV positive and when they become ill, their families and children bear the burden alone.
Children and partners also have to deal with the grief of watching a loved one suffer and die.
Research has found that most families who lost someone, spent about one year nursing the person once they became seriously ill.
Counselling without treatment and nutrition will not keep someone alive.
Clinic treatment without home-based care will not provide for people once they are bed-ridden.
There are many examples of well-integrated projects from all over the world:
In Sao Paolo in Brazil,Catholic nuns
started Project Hope to provide support and care for families affected by AIDS.
They have more than 100 volunteers who each give a few hours of their time per week.
The volunteers each visit a few families where parents are ill. They provide basic care, counselling and help care for children.
The project also looks after children once their parents have died.
In many parts of Africa, health services work closely with community and church volunteers to care for people who are ill - especially in rural areas that are far from other services.
Chirumhanza (Zimbabwe), Kitui (Kenya) and Kikovo (Uganda)
are good examples of places where health services extend the care and support they can give by using home-based care.
In South Africa there are also many projects that do very good work. Most of them work with a local hospital or clinic.
Affected families are offered support and trained volunteers visit them at home. When people need medicines, grants and other support, the volunteers help them to get access to those things.
The Tateni Home Care Services in Mamelodi and the Hospice project in Port Shepstone are two of the oldest home-care projects.
In Thailand, the Sanpatong Family Care Project does home-based care and helps to set up support groups for people living with HIV and AIDS and their families.
Being active is good for you in lots of ways – it can help to build your muscles, keep your bones strong, burn fat and keep your heart healthy.
Some people who are living with HIV experience
loss of muscle mass and strength
, so exercise can help prevent this.
You might get your exercise by
taking part in a sport, or going to the gym, but everyday activities like dancing, walking and gardening
can all help get you moving. If you want to do more exercise, feel fitter, have more stamina, more flexibility, or lose weight, there are three types of exercise to think about. These include:
Cardio or aerobic exercise

– 
this increases your heart rate to help blood flow right around your body, delivering oxygen to your muscles and keeping your heart and lungs healthy. Try running, swimming, dancing or cycling
Resistance training

–
 this increases the strength of your muscles by lifting weights for a period of time and then repeating. Even lifting a tin of beans will do!
Flexibility training

– 
this stretches different parts of your body to strengthen your muscles and joints. Try stretching before and after any exercise you do, or focus on flexibility with an activity like yoga.
Staying happy and fulfilling your potential
Taking care of yourself is not just about your physical health, but looking after your mental and emotional health too.

Finding out you have HIV can be a shock, and it may take you some time to adjust. Support from your friends and family, or other people living with HIV, can really help when you are finding things difficult.
Once you begin coming to terms with HIV, it’s a good idea to think about the rest of your life, i.e.
What are your goals?
What’s important to you?
Maybe you want to study, have a family, travel or change career – HIV shouldn’t stop you doing any of these things!
What else can I do to take care of myself?
Many of the things we do to look after ourselves are common sense. Try to get plenty of rest and sleep.
If you smoke, try to stop
it isn’t always easy, but there is support available to help you.
If you are concerned about your alcohol or drug use , talk to a healthcare professional for advice and support.
It’s also important to think about any other health conditions you have; particularly as we get older, we’re more likely to experience other health problems.
Exercising
Youths should be encouraged to do a lot of exercising.
They do not have to belong to any gym, but they can exercise at home as individuals or start their own club at their own time.
Time can be set aside on some days for exercising during support group days, an hour will be enough.
When you exercise you also produce more blood cells, which means a better immune system.
Swimming
is very good exercise and you can go trying it.
Dancing
is a great way to get exercise without feeling it. Put on the radio or play a CD that the group members like.
When you dance you will also feel “happy” and your body will benefit from the extra oxygen it will receive.
Oxygen
also helps kill infections.
Exercise is also a good way to help reduce mental stress and anxiety.
Too much stress and anxiety can cause a breakdown of the immune system.
Yoga and other stretch exercises are also excellent methods to de-stress the mind and strengthen the body.
Since the late 1980s, researchers have attempted to cure HIV infection. However, in the first two decades of the AIDS epidemic, such efforts were largely dangerous and unsuccessful.
HIV cure research to date has focused on clearing the virus from
T cells
, a type of
white blood cell
that is an essential part of the immune system.
Yet investigators have found the virus persists in HIV-infected
macrophages
Macrophages
are large white blood cells found in tissues throughout the body including the liver, lung, bone marrow and brain.
The discovery of this additional viral reservoir has significant implications for HIV cure research.
The journey toward a cure will not be easy and many challenges lie ahead. Some of the challenges are known, others may only become known as experiments proceed.
As with any great scientific endeavour, there will be
setbacks.
This means that research funding agencies and the public need to be patient while utilizing HIV Testing and Adherence to prevent HIV transmision as the journey towards cure goes on.
The initial wave of cure research experiments over the next five years should be viewed as exploratory and their results preliminary.
This research will seek to answer important scientific questions that can then be used to build a foundation as researchers work toward a cure.

PrEP and PEP today
PEP must start within 72 hours
of a possible exposure and is taken for 28 days. PrEP now also includes long-acting injectable options (CAB-LA, lenacapavir) and the dapivirine ring.
U = U — Undetectable = Untransmittable.
Someone on HIV treatment with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV to sexual partners. This is backed by global scientific consensus (WHO, CDC, UNAIDS).
How is (PrEP) different from (PEP)?

PrEP is not the same as PEP (which stands for Post-Exposure Prophylaxis). While both are taken by HIV-negative people to prevent HIV, PrEP is taken to reduce the risk of getting HIV from the potential exposure that may occur sometime in the future. It should be taken once every day so when a person comes in contact with HIV, his or her body is ready to fight off the virus. PrEP should be taken continuously for as long as a person remains at high risk of HIV (for example, when one’s partner is HIVpositive, or when a person has multiple sex partners).

PEP, on the other hand, is taken only after a person might have been exposed to HIV (for example a condom broke or was not used with a partner who is possibly HIVpositive, or a person was raped). PEP has to be started within 3 days after possible

HIV exposure and involves taking a full treatment dose of ARV drugs two or three times a day for 28 days. Because of the higher dose of ARVs, side effects are more common with PEP than with PrEP, and these side effects are more pronounced.
PEP is a good choice for those who may experience rare, accidental exposure to HIV, while PrEP is a good choice for people who have an ongoing high risk of HIV exposure.

Is there evidence for PrEP?
Large research studies, including some done in Kenya show that PrEP reduces new HIV infections by more than 90% if taken every day.

PrEP has been shown to work in rigorous clinical trials and also during demonstration ‘real world’

Why PrEP?
HIV is to be a big problem in Kenya, as we continue to have many new infections every year despite efforts at HIV prevention.

How does PrEP work?
If you are exposed to HIV, these medicines can stop the virus from multiplying and spreading throughout your body.
PrEP only works if you have enough medicine in your body, so you need to take PrEP every day.
Who is PrEP for?
PrEP is not for everyone, but may be a suitable prevention method for many people at risk of acquiring HIV.
Some of these people could include serodiscordant couples, and people who have sex with someone of unknown HIV status.
Remember that PrEP is for use only in HIV negative individuals

What is a Parent/Child Relationship?

The Parent/Child Relations is a special type of a bond that arises between a caregiver and a child. It consists of a combination of behaviors, feelings, and expectations that are unique to a particular parent and a particular child. Of the many different relationships people form over the course of the life span, the relationship between parent and child is among the most important. The quality of the parent-child relationship can be affected by the parent's age, experience, or self-confidence; the stability of the parents' marriage; and the unique characteristics of the child compared with those of the parent.
FACTORS THAT CAN INFLUENCE THE PARENT/CHILD RELATIONSHIP
At times the parent/child relationship can face many challenges:
Death of a parent
Illness of the parent or the child
Divorce and re-marriage Financial problems Misunderstanding due to age/generation differences. For example, differences in lifestyle, dressing, behavior, or some cultural practices
Transition from childhood to adulthood
How can I help my child to improve adherence to their medication?

For any person, taking medication is not always easy. At times, we can forget or have issues come up that make us not take medication. It’s good to have a strategy of making it more friendly, like taking the medicines together. You can be your child’s medicine buddy. A medicine buddy can remind someone to take medicines and reward the person if medicines are taken daily!
How can I have a good relationship with my child?
Most relationships thrive when there is room for growth. Below are important considerations for parents to enhance a good relationship:
Interact with your child.
Read nonverbal communication.
Follow your child’s interests.
How can I continue having a good relationship with my child as she/he enters adolescence?

As a child transitions to adulthood, this stage is called adolescence. In adolescence, so many things happen that can affect your relationship. There are physical, emotional, social, and mental changes that take place during this stage, including the desire for more independence. Many parents find early adolescence a difficult period. Adolescents fare best and their parents are happiest when parents can be both encouraging and accepting of the child's needs for more psychological independence.
Communicate with kindness and respect

Young teens can say or do things that are outrageous, mean-spirited, or both. However hard your child pushes your buttons, it's best to respond calmly. The respect and self-control that you display in talks with your child may some day be reflected in her conversations with others. The key is being understanding as well as balancing the need for independence and good guidance.
How can I start disclosing about HIV to my child?

Establishing a good relationship with your child from an early age will give you a strong ground to be open about issues that will affect their lives. Ideally, a parent could be open in this relationship, even if they are not giving the child all of the information yet. Disclosure is a process and one needs to be physically and emotionally strong for the process. The first step is being open and honest.
When will my child be ready for disclosure?

When children get to the adolescent stage, they are more aware of their environment, their bodies, and their lives. Therefore, it’s important to start this process when they first become more aware about themselves. You can tell this stage is starting when the child begins asking many questions
My child asks so many questions, how do I answer them?

Listen to the questions your child is asking and always have something positive to say. Most children will ask, “Why am I taking medicines when am not sick? Why don't other children take medicines daily and yet I do?” Often as a parent you will have an inclination to lie so they stop asking many questions, but that may lead to distrust when they know the truth. We encourage you to be honest and to be positive.
What if my child blames me for giving him/her HIV?

Remember that you are not a bad parent. You have made a positive decision to take care of your health and your child’s health. Although sometimes HIV can be acquired as a consequence of a bad decision made by yourself or by your partner, like your child, you didn’t choose to have HIV! When you feel overcome with shame and guilt, it may lead to stress, and you may not be able to help your child during disclosure. One strategy for addressing your child’s blame is to remind the child how much you love them, and that is why you are disclosing to them now. It is important for your child to understand their HIV status so they can live positively and grow up healthy. The fact that you are telling your child they are HIV positive means that you love them.

Definitions
Boyfriend/Girlfriend
A boyfriend/girlfriend is a term that is typically used to describe a relationship with a close friend of the opposite sex when romantic feelings are involved
PARTNERS
Partner is another word for a boyfriend or a girlfriend. This term is often used to describe someone who is in a serious, committed relationship.
Romantic Relationships
A romantic relationship is a relationship with someone from the opposite sex to whom you have emotional attraction.
Is it normal to feel attracted to a boy or a girl of the opposite sex?

Because you are young, it’s good to develop your relationship in a healthy manner. A healthy relationship with a person of the opposite sex includes being open with one another and building trust with one another. It’s important to talk about important things that you would wish to happen in your lives and set priorities for what you would wish to achieve. Remember to:
Be open to one another
Take care of one another.
What do I do when I feel like I want to kiss and hug someone from the opposite sex?

It’s important to understand that attraction hormones develop while you are an adolescent. Sometimes, relationships with people from the opposite sex can increase in intensity and you may trust the person enough to engage in sexual behaviors. You may feel confused what to do when you feel you would wish to explore sex and intimate actions such as kissing and hugging with someone else. Although it can be difficult, it’s very important not to have sex until you are married and old enough to take responsibility for the outcome of sex.
You can consider the following strategies to help you with sexual temptations:
Always plan to meet with your boyfriend/girlfriend in an open place, or at a place where there are other people
Engage in activities that help you physically, emotionally and socially such as sports, hiking, camping, mental exercises like puzzles.
Avoid watching movies or programs that are of adult nature or that make you excited sexually.
Avoid listening to friends who advise you to have sex before marriage.
When you have questions about your relationship, ask for advice from your parents or any other close older person who loves you
Romantic Relationship Considerations

When you are in a romantic relationship with someone, you should consider the following three factors before engaging in sexual intercourse or other sexual behaviors. Please see our pamphlet on Sexual Intercourse and talk to your counselor for more information about sex.
Abstinence in Your Relationship

Abstinence means restraining from participating in sexual behaviors. You are in charge of your own actions, so you can set a goal to not engage in sexual acts with other people, or practice abstinence. By practicing abstinence, you greatly reduce your chances of contracting a sexually transmitted infection.
Protection in Your Relationship

If you and your partner have made the decision to engage in sexual acts, please use protection such as condoms. Condoms can help protect not only you, but also your partner, from sexually transmitted infections and unplanned pregnancy. It is important not only to protect yourself from such infections from sex, but also that you protect your partner from such infections.
Faithfulness in Your Relationship

If you and your partner have engaged in sexual acts, you should discuss being faithful to one another and not having multiple sexual partners at one time. If you have multiple sexual partners at one time and you do not use protection, you could endanger yourself and your partners with sexually transmitted infections or unwanted pregnancies. Remaining faithful to one partner reduces the likelihood of getting a sexually transmitted infection. Faithfulness also strengthens the relationship you have with your partner with trust and honesty.

People with HIV can engage in sexual intercourse. However, it is true that HIV can be passed from one person to another through sexual intercourse. Protection should be used to prevent transmission of HIV and to prevent contracting or spreading other sexually transmitted infections. If your partner is not ready for sex, then they have the right to refuse sexual acts.
Definitions
Sexual Intercourse

Sexual intercourse is a physical act that involves close contact with genitals. Most often, people think of sexual intercourse as a male’s penis entering a female’s vagina. During this contact, vaginal fluids and semen are exchanged. These fluids can carry sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhea, chlamydia, genital warts, etc.) and the HIV virus. Other forms of sexual intercourse (listed below) can also result in sexually transmitted infections:
Oral Sex:
the sexual act of stimulating the genitalia of a partner with the mouth.
Anal Sex:
the sexual act of inserting the male’s penis into the anus.
What is a sexually transmitted infection?

A sexually transmitted infection is an infection that is passed from one person to another through sexual behaviors. Sexually transmitted infections can cause some physical symptoms such as rashes, boils, discharge from genitalia, or aches. These infections can also be “invisible” and not show any signs of infection. Protection during sexual behaviors, such as using condoms, can protect you from contracting such infections.
Human Sexual Response Cycle:
When humans are engaged in sexual activity, their body goes through several stages, called the Human Sexual Response Cycle:
Excitement:
Increase in heart rate and breathing
Arousal:
genitals may swell. For males, the penis will become erect, and for females the genitals may become sensitive and lubricated.
Plateau Phase:
Occurs right before orgasm.
Orgasmic Phase:
Contraction of lower pelvic muscles and a release of fluids from the genitals. Males release semen at this time, which is called ejaculation.
Resolution Phase:
Muscles begin to relax, the heart rate lowers, and the penis returns to a normal state of being flaccid and non-erect.
Transmission
What are the risks of having sex?
Consequences of having sex may include:
Pregnancy
Sexually Transmitted infections
Increase in HIV infection
Dropping out of school
Having a bad image
Can I give someone else HIV? If so, how?

If you have HIV, you can give your partner HIV through unprotected sexual intercourse. This means you do not use a condom to prevent the exchange of fluids. The HIV virus is transmitted in bodily fluids.

Take your medications according to your prescription regimen. By taking your medicines and remaining healthy, there is less HIV virus in your fluids and it will be less likely that you pass the virus to your partner.
How do I know if my partner has a sexually transmitted infection?

Some sexually transmitted infections do not show any symptoms, so it is difficult to tell if people have infections. You can go to a clinic to get tested for sexually transmitted infections. If you have questions about where to get tested, please contact your counselor. 
If you and your partner have not been tested, you should always use protection, such as condoms, to prevent transmission of “invisible” sexually transmitted infections.
Why do people use condoms?

Condoms are a tool used to protect yourself and your partner during sexual intercourse. A condom is usually made of rubber and is made to cover the male penis, preventing the transmission of fluids from one partner to the other during sexual intercourse.
 Condoms must be used appropriately in order to be effective. If you are unsure of how to use a condom, please see your clinical officer or counselor at the clinic for an instruction.
When do you use a condom?

You should use a condom or make sure your partner puts on a condom, appropriately, before ANY contact with his or her genitals. The penis should be erect before applying the condom, to prevent any slippage of the condom.
How do you use a condom?
*IMPORTANT:

The condom’s prevention of transmission of fluids is only successful if it is used appropriately. If there are any tears in the condom, then it is not going to prevent or block any fluids from your partner, and provides no protection.
Inspect the condom wrapper to ensure there are no tears in either the condom or the condom wrapper, and that the condom is not expired.
Open the condom by tearing the edge of the condom wrapper.
Determine which way the condom is rolled. This can be done easily by feeling with your fingers which way the condom unrolls.
Pinch the reservoir tip so enough space is left at the tip of the penis and roll the condom with your forefinger and thumb down the shaft of the erect penis.

During sexual intercourse, be keen on any rips or tears in the condom. If you notice a rip or tear, immediately withdraw the penis from your partner, remove the spoilt condom and put a new one on the penis.

Immediately after ejaculation, withdraw the penis and remove the condom by grabbing the end of the condom, ensuring that the fluid inside does not spill out. To prevent the condom contents from spilling, you can tie a knot at the end of the condom before disposal into the trash.

If you plan to have sex, always ensure your partner is willing to engage in sexual intercourse. You should only engage in sexual acts with someone you KNOW and TRUSTs. There are many emotions that are involved with sex and it is a topic and act that should not be taken lightly.

Latest guidance
All pregnant women with HIV start lifelong ART immediately (treat-all). With a sustained undetectable viral load, mother-to-child transmission drops below 1%.
On infant feeding, guidance depends on setting:
WHO recommends breastfeeding while on suppressive ART where formula is not safe and sustainable; formula-only advice applies mainly to high-income settings.
What factors increase the chance of transmission from mother to baby?
Transmission of any infectious matter (including HIV) depends upon three factors:
How infectious it is
How efficient the route of transmission is
How vulnerable the potential 'recipient' is
Factors which increase the likelihood of transmission of HIV from mother to baby include:

A high viral load, especially during labour and delivery. A mother with high viral load is more likely to transmit HIV, and transmission is most likely to occur during labour and delivery. However, though transmission is rare in mothers with undetectable viral load, it does still occur.
A low CD4 count or CD4 percentage.
Advanced HIV disease or previous AIDS-defining illness.
Older age of mother.
Smoking during pregnancy.
Use of recreational or illegal drugs during pregnancy.
Frequent unprotected sex, especially with multiple partners, during pregnancy.
No HIV therapy during pregnancy or delivery.
Premature delivery.
Waters breaking more than four hours before delivery.
Prolonged or difficult labour.
Cervical or vaginal infection (e.g. bacterial vaginosis).
Breastfeeding or mixed feeding (breast or formula).
The mother having another illness, such as TB or malaria, can increase the chance of transmission by elevating viral load or by causing immune activation.
What is mother-to-child transmission of HIV?

Mother-to-child transmission of HIV is the spread of HIV from an HIV-infected woman to her child during pregnancy, childbirth (also called labor and delivery), or breastfeeding (through breast milk). Mother-to-child transmission of HIV is also called perinatal transmission of HIV.
Mother-to-child transmission is the most common way that children become infected with HIV.
Can mother-to-child transmission of HIV be prevented?
Yes.
Because of the use of HIV medicines and other strategies, the risk of mother-to-child transmission can be lowered to 1% or less.
The risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV is low when:
HIV is detected as early as possible during pregnancy (or before a woman gets pregnant).
Women with HIV receive HIV medicine during pregnancy and childbirth and, in certain situations, have a scheduled cesarean delivery (sometimes called a C-section).
Babies born to women with HIV receive HIV medicines for 4 to 6 weeks after birth and are not breastfed.
Is HIV testing recommended for pregnant women?
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
recommends that all women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant get tested for HIV as early as possible—before, if possible, and during every pregnancy.
Pregnant women with HIV receive HIV medicines to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and to protect their own health.
HIV medicines are recommended for everyone infected with HIV. HIV medicines help people with HIV live longer, healthier lives and reduce the risk of transmission of HIV.
How do HIV medicines prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV?
HIV medicines work by preventing HIV from multiplying, which reduces the amount of HIV in the body.
Having less HIV in the body reduces a woman's risk of passing HIV to her child during pregnancy and childbirth. Having less HIV in the body also protects the woman's health.
Some of the HIV medicine passes from the pregnant woman to her unborn baby across the placenta (also called the afterbirth).

This transfer of HIV medicine protects the baby from HIV infection, especially during a vaginal delivery when the baby passes through the birth canal and is exposed to any HIV in the mother’s blood or other fluids.
In some situations, a woman with HIV may have a cesarean delivery (sometimes called a
C-section
) to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV during delivery.
Babies born to women with HIV receive HIV medicine for 4 to 6 weeks after birth.
The HIV medicine reduces the risk of infection from any HIV that may have entered a baby’s body during childbirth.
Are HIV medicines safe to use during pregnancy?
Most HIV medicines are safe to use during pregnancy.
In general, HIV medicines don’t increase the risk of birth defects.
Health care providers talk with HIV-infected women about the benefits and risks of specific HIV medicines to help the women decide which HIV medicines to use during pregnancy.
Are there other ways to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV?
Because HIV can be transmitted in breast milk, HIV-infected women in the United States should not breastfeed their babies.
In the United States, baby formula is a safe and healthy alternative to breast milk.
There are reports of children becoming infected with HIV by eating food that was previously chewed by a person infected with HIV.
To be safe, babies should not be fed pre-chewed food.
